clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear regression models exploring relationships between extreme functional connections and clinical characteristics (symptom severity, illness duration, age of onset) with Bonferroni correction (p<0.05). Functional enrichment analysis associating extreme connections with 217 cognitive/functional terms using Neurosynth data, evaluated with permutation testing (10,000 iterations). Two-sample t-tests comparing subtypes to HCs, controlling for sex, age, study site, and head motion (mean FD), with Bonferroni correction (p<0.05). K-means clustering with SigClust validation; cluster ensemble voting (26 indices) to determine optimal number of subtypes. Linear SVMs for case-control classification (100×10-fold cross-validation framework); accuracy significance determined using 100 random label permutations; performance differences between models compared using two-sample t-tests with Bonferroni correction.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two robust MDD subtypes were identified with contrasting functional connectivity patterns: subtype 1 (N=394) showed overall increased connectivity while subtype 2 (N=882) showed decreased connectivity, both relative to HCs, despite similar clinical presentations; these subtypes significantly improved case-control classification accuracy (71.66% and 63.26% vs. 55.10% for all patients) and showed 92.92% discriminability between subtypes.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study identified 556 extreme functional connections (consistency rate >95%) in MDD patients, predominantly between visual network and frontoparietal/DMN/ventral attention networks, with key nodes in anterior cingulate cortex, bilateral orbitofrontal cortex, and supramarginal gyrus. These extreme connections were significantly enriched for reward, motivation, and pain processes (permutation p<0.05) and associated with age of onset (adjusted R²=0.39, F=2.13, Bonferroni p<0.01). K-means clustering identified two subtypes: Subtype 1 (N=394) exhibited overall increased functional connectivity in 19,579 of 19,900 connections, with pronounced abnormalities in visual network and between visual-DMN/frontoparietal/ventral attention networks; Subtype 2 (N=882) showed overall decreased connectivity in 15,405 connections with similar network distribution. Combined analysis of all patients showed no significant differences (Bonferroni p<0.05). Subtypes did not differ in demographic or clinical characteristics (age, sex, illness duration, HAMD, episode status, medication status; all p>0.05), though illness duration difference approached significance (p=0.07). Classification accuracy was 71.66% for Subtype 1 vs. HCs (Bonferroni p<0.01), 63.26% for Subtype 2 vs. HCs (Bonferroni p<0.01), compared to 55.10% for all patients vs. HCs; inter-subtype accuracy was 92.92%. Cluster stability index was 0.39 for subsampling and 0.44 for leave-one-site-out validation (both permutation p<0.01). Results were robust to parameter variations (90% consistency threshold: ARI=0.97, 94.00% inter-subtype accuracy) and medication status (untreated patients showed similar patterns with higher classification accuracy: 83.05% and 70.39% vs. 63.01% for all untreated). Disease-specificity analysis showed distinct extreme connection profiles in schizophrenia patients (COBRE dataset), confirming MDD-specific patterns.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Only cross-sectional data analyzed, raising questions about subtype stability over time; limited clinical data prevented examination of reward processing and other potential subtype differences; confounding factors (smoking, drinking) not available; only patients without comorbid mental disorders included, so impact of comorbidities unexplored
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: This study has several limitations. First, only cross-sectional data were analyzed, which raises questions about the stability of the identified subtypes over time. Longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the robustness of our findings and explore the subtypes' responses to treatment and disease progression. Second, the limited clinical data available prevented us from examining other potential differences between subtypes, such as those related to reward processing. Future research should aim to gather more comprehensive clinical data to better characterize the subtypes. Third, confounding factors including the smoking and drinking were not available and their effects on the findings warrant further investigation. Finally, only patients without comorbid mental disorders were included, so the impact of comorbidities on the identified subtypes remains unexplored.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study used a tolerance interval-based approach to identify subject-level abnormalities, which does not require predefined regions of interest, complex models, or preset parameters. Enrichment analysis based on hypergeometric cumulative distribution function was used to identify connections significantly more prevalent in MDD patients vs. HCs. The cluster ensemble voting technique considers 26 indices to assess clustering quality and determine optimal number of subtypes. For comparison, group-level abnormal connections were also identified using standard t-tests, which yielded distinct spatial distributions and lower cluster stability (0.31 for subsampling, 0.35 for leave-one-site-out) compared to tolerance interval-based features. Disease-specificity was validated by applying the same pipeline to schizophrenia patients (COBRE dataset, N=72 patients, 74 HCs), revealing distinct extreme connection profiles.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a large multi-site study from the REST-meta-MDD consortium (25 sites, 1276 MDD patients, 1104 HCs). The paper uses a novel application of tolerance intervals for normative modeling in functional connectivity, identifying subject-level deviations rather than group-level averages. Notably, the SD for HC age reported in the text (24.55 years) appears inconsistent with the MDD age SD in Table 1 (14.62 years); this may be a typographical error. The consistency rate approach (repeating feature selection 100 times with 90% subsampling) is a robust method for identifying reproducible features. The study included both first-episode (538) and recurrent (282) patients, as well as untreated (447) and treated (408) patients, with unknown status for episodicity (456) and medication (421). Clinical characteristics: HAMD mean 20.50±7.66, illness duration 36.46±59.68 months, age of onset 31.97±11.95 years. The finding that combined analysis showed no significant differences while subtype-specific analyses revealed contrasting patterns (hyper- vs. hypo-connectivity) provides important insights into MDD heterogeneity and may explain conflicting findings in the literature.
